description: We are passionate about space, science, and building intelligent systems from real-world data. Our strengths include machine learning, computer vision, data science, and rapid prototyping. For NASA Space Apps, we want to turn NASA data into a useful, technically strong, and memorable solution with real mission value.
summary:
Rocky is a walk planner for the first astronauts on Mars. It answers the one question a crew outside the habitat must always be able to answer: can we still walk home?

Apollo crews followed a rule: never go farther than you can walk back. Rocky turns that rule into a map of a real place, Curiosity's boxwork site on Mount Sharp in Gale crater, built from NASA and USGS 1 m terrain. Every 3 m square shows how much suit time would be left after walking home from it, using published models of suited walking at Mars gravity.

Crews plan a route to real Curiosity science targets and see the safety margin at every step. Rocky picks the walk with the most science that still gets the crew home, and drills the worst days: a solar storm, or a partner who collapses and must be hauled back.

We checked it against Mars itself: our radiation shelter map against Curiosity's own detector at 1,298 rover stops, and our walking model against NASA's suited treadmill tests, within 13% on average.

On Mars, nobody comes to get you. Rocky shows the way home.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Rocky is a walk planner for the first crews on Mars. It keeps answering one question: can we still walk home?

The site is a 3.2 km square at Curiosity's boxwork on Mount Sharp, Gale crater, built from the USGS 1 m elevation model and HiRISE imagery. We turn it into a grid of 1.14 million squares of 3 m. For each step, Rocky computes walking speed (Marquez 2008) and effort (Santee 2001) at Mars gravity, for a suited astronaut carrying a load. Slopes over 20° are closed. A shortest-path search from the habitat gives every square its walk home and the suit time left on arrival. The rule: at every point of a walk, the crew must be able to turn back and arrive with at least 20% left.

On top of that:

- Plan: place stops at real Curiosity targets and get a verdict. Our demo walk (4 stops, 2.04 km, 2 h 55 min) never drops below 51%.

- Best science: Rocky tries all 2,048 combinations of 11 targets and keeps the richest walk that still gets home.

- Habitat siting: scores 3,372 candidate sites by the science one safe walk can reach.

- Worst-day drills: a solar storm (can the crew reach shelter before the particles arrive?) and a collapsed partner (one astronaut hauls the other home).

- Radiation layer: next to a cliff, part of the sky is hidden, so less cosmic radiation reaches you. Rocky computes this from the terrain.

- 3D walk, helmet view, and Mars on your table in AR.

- Every number on screen is marked measured, computed or assumed.

HOW WE CHECKED IT

- Radiation: our sky-blocking matches a 2026 peer-reviewed study of Curiosity's stops at r = 0.993. Against Curiosity's own detector at 1,298 stops (365,761 readings over 13 years), Rocky gets the direction right 89% of the time where shelter is large. It overestimates the size, and the app shows the corrected value.

- Walking: on 9 NASA suited treadmill tests (121 kg suit), our model is within 13% on average.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Crews and mission planners get a clear go or no-go before the hatch opens, the most science per walk without trading away safety, and rehearsed plans for the worst day. Planners can compare habitat and landing sites with the same rule the crew will follow. The method needs only an elevation model, so it can move to Jezero and the human landing candidates.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Apollo's walk-back rule was one distance on a checklist; we turned it into a map where every spot knows the way home. And instead of trusting our own model, we used Curiosity as a test astronaut: it carried a radiation meter for 13 years, so we asked it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

NASA's own limits (6-hour EVAs and 20° slopes from Artemis planning, Apollo's walk-back rule), suit mass and carried loads, the heavier return with samples, Mars gravity, radiation and space weather, and being honest about limits. The hauling pace (0.5 m/s) and the storm warning time (30 min) are our assumptions, labelled in the app.

TOOLS

TypeScript, React, Vite, three.js, CesiumJS and WebXR for the web app. Python (NumPy, SciPy, Numba, rasterio, cdflib) for the data pipeline. Data from NASA, JPL and USGS: JPL Mars Trek, Mars Perseverance Raw Images, the Gale 1 m elevation mosaic, HiRISE imagery, Curiosity RAD data and waypoints, REMS weather, THEMIS, the DONKI space-weather database, and NASA technical reports on suited walking. No special hardware: it runs in a browser.
